terms: the mill: The main employer in Elk River, when it went out, everything was gone and men worked the woods or shipped lumber by train. ; Forest Service: Husbands worked for it before other ventures, it is where local young men go if not logging, and its newcomers changed the towns. ; Potlatch lumber company = PFI | Potlatch Timber Company | the Potlatch: The company—later Potlatch Corporation—that owned the town, ran its hospital, fed needy families in the Depression, and moved men between camps. ; flunky = flunkies: A cook's assistant for the forestry service and camp kitchens, the only women allowed in logging camp were the flunkies who waited tables. ; fire patrol: Her husband worked four years for the fire patrol, she worked in the fire patrol kitchen making sandwiches for firefighters flown out by plane. ; University of Montana ranger's course = University of Montana: Where a husband took the ranger's course with fare, books and tuition paid while they lived on five dollars a week. ; cook house: At the Fernwood mill camp her mother took meals there, presided over by a former camp cook who resented furnishing extras. ; forest fire: A big fire near Elk River when Norma was a newborn, residents were told to gather at the riverbank if the town burned. ; coasting: In her childhood everyone went coasting on sleds in winter, which children no longer do. ; saw mills = small sawmill: Where her ex-husband always worked, two uncles also ran a small family saw mill with a big mill pond for barbecues. ; big cedars: Great trees in the swampy bear wallow near the homestead that locals used as a landmark on trips. ; sawyer: The first man in felling a tree, a dangerous but well-paid job Mrs. Larson's husband loved. ; Cortland Mill Company: Her father managed its Fernwood sawmill in 1925, running three eight-hour shifts before the company folded. ; making shakes = permit for shakes: She and her grandson split wooden shakes to shingle their cabin, but after fifty years of taking fallen cedar, getting a permit took a whole summer. ; Wild and Scenic Rivers Act = Walden City Rivers Act: The association fights Forest Service management of the valley under the act, she wants to rebut Reader's Digest's praise of it. ; fire school: Hundreds of boys came from all over to fire school, standing five deep in cold rain to be fed. ; log drive: Her father told of bringing a log drive down to Kansas past a railroad bridge. ; Troy Lumber Company: After helping another cook, she became head cook in logging camps and at its mill at the white pine. ; 980: The machine her husband operates for PFI, work he likes better than anything else he has done. ; blister rust work: In 1934 her new husband did blister rust work in the woods at Pierce for $125 a month. ; Forest Service camps: Her brothers worked for the Forest Service in summers, and her husband cooked in Forest Service camps and sheep camps. ; hooking: The speaker's two oldest sons work in the woods as loggers, mainly hooking. ; bunkhouses: Logging camp housing with four men to each bunkhouse where workers played practical jokes. ; Creig Mountain Lumber Company: It moved Camp 6 where her school was and wanted her to teach the winter school too. ; crullers: One of the sweets the camp kitchen sometimes set out for the men to pack into their lunches. ; deserted logging camps: Big companies like Weyerhaeuser left dishes and windows behind because packing them out cost more than leaving them. ; Diamond Match: Her husband later worked several years for it. ; double saws on either end of the carriage: Machine used to make rails by cutting them at both ends simultaneously. ; fish hatchery: New arrivals include educated people who came to work on the fish hatchery and for the Forest Service. ; giant stride: The camp playground's was a topped jack-pine with a greased wagon wheel and ropes, improvised at no cost. ; green window shades: Used as blackboards in the one-room camp school, the teacher's chalk writing was still on them 30 years later. ; making ties by hand: Most men near Troy made a living hewing railroad ties by hand with an old ax for the unfinished Great Northern. ; Milwaukie Lumber Company: Company her husband scaled timber for, which moved its logging operation from Fernwood up to Alder Creek. ; saw horse desks = saw horses: High carpenter's saw horses served as desks and low ones as seats in the one-room homestead school. ; speeder: The rail vehicle that was supposed to carry her husband in from camp when the baby was being born. ; spring layoff = layoff in the spring: Woods work has layoffs of at least two months in spring and again in fall, making it hard for families to leave. ; spring thaw: Spring thaw stops logging work because roads get torn up and logs cannot be skidded. ; stull yard: Her father ran a stull yard in Plummer, which she explains was like a pole yard of today. ; timber cruising: Her husband's self-employed work after Forest Service retirement, making timber estimates and surveying. ; whip log: The single log her seven-year-old had to cross over the river to reach school from the logging camp.

strike: During a long strike the whole town painted the buildings, then ate hot dogs and danced in the blocked-off street. ; smelter smoke = smelter | SO2 | sulfur dioxide: Kellogg narrators recall smelter fumes rotting screen doors and burning leaves, one shrugs off lead-poisoning claims as hooey. ; Bunker Hill: Speakers and husbands worked its offices, zinc plant and contract stopes, its topsoil finally made one woman's garden grow. ; the smelter: A father works up there repairing pipes as a lead burner, town women can now take jobs at the smelter or in offices. ; Sunshine disaster = Sunshine fire | mine disaster: Her husband was in the Sunshine fire, she interviewed the mining wives for a Boise State study, and a friend took in boarders after her husband was killed. ; Tupperware: She sells Tupperware in Kellogg to meet people, with local dealers covering each other's parties for commission. ; contract miner = contract miners: A contract miner is paid per amount of ore brought out, like a commission, earning more the more ore he gets. ; my mine and hospital shifts = 3-11 shifts: Shifting mine and hospital schedules like the 3-11 shift keep married couples from seeing each other, a reason one narrator quit work. ; lead burner: The narrator's father is a lead burner, a welder-like trade working with lead, repairing pipes at the smelter. ; smelter mill: In Missouri her father worked at a smelter mill and a junkyard, jobs that kept the family going. ; salt pills: Miners take salt pills underground to avoid heat exhaustion, and get heat cramps if they skip them. ; Haccoff Mining Company: Her husband was timberchief during the Depression, his wages were cut but he never missed a payday. ; Pickwick Grocery: She previously worked part time at this Kellogg grocery. ; skip tender: Before becoming a miner her husband worked as a skip tender on the conveyance that takes lumber down to the miners.

combine: Now they combine, but then they had threshing crews. ; homesteading = homesteading in Montana | prove up: Women proved up claims alone, riding in twice a year or living winters on the land while husbands worked away, homesteading life was fun but kerosene lamps lost out to electricity. ; thrashing: For ten years they thrashed grain with combines while she cooked for the crews alone with three small children. ; driving truck = drove a grain truck: As the only girl she gets stuck driving truck on the farm, another drove a grain truck among her jobs. ; squirrel: She had pet squirrels that slept in her pockets. ; thrashing machine: Fourteen or fifteen men came at threshing time with pitchforks and wagons, during the Depression they hired out with the thrashing machine. ; trapping: A lot of men trapped then, her husband fell in with an old trapper and made pretty good money at it. ; homestead cabin = homestead house: A small 18-by-28 house with a loft floor for a bed, Dan later joined two of them into one big white house. ; wheat farm: Her father's Genesee farm raised only wheat with no animals, so the children had few chores beyond dishes after dinner. ; cooperative work = neighbors helped neighbors | neighbors showed up: Neighbors helped neighbors: farm wives crossed the road at haying time, shared food at picnics, and finished each other's combining when a husband fell ill. ; crosscut: She learned how to do crosscut work and goes up to the woods to work with her husband doing it. ; cream separator: She separated milk first with a hand-turned separator, then an electric one, and hated washing it afterwards. ; cistern: The farm had one when they moved there, but they got rid of it in a hurry because the water was not good. ; cookhouse: She made butter and canned fruit in two-quart jars to feed the harvest cookhouse and cut expenses. ; dust mulch = dust mulch idea: A brand-new dry-farming method in the late 1800s that let one man thresh twelve bushels of wheat per acre on the plains. ; squaw corn = squall corn: A short field corn with several ears to the stalk, grown before sweet corn was known there. ; creamery: Where they sold the cream for butter. ; homesteads: Old homesteads of hewed logs built right on the ground with cedar-shake roofs, slowly decaying from the bottom up. ; loose hay: Before balers, the family hayed all summer with loose hay, the children expected to help rather than take summer jobs. ; raised fryers: Rather than keeping many chickens for eggs, they mostly raised fryers for meat. ; threshing rig = steam engine: They came with a steam engine and a threshing rig. ; skunks: Skunks killed chickens by sucking their blood, their hides now fetch $28, and her grandchildren trap them. ; schoolhouse sat right here by the Grange Hall: Country schools at Teakean, Cavendish, Cream Ridge, and Southwick served small farm families before consolidation closed them. ; cook wagon: In the rainy 1920 harvest she set bread while it moved, peeled vegetables en route, and shoveled mud off the floor. ; hunting dogs: They keep eight to fourteen hunting dogs fed on trimmed bones, wounded bears sometimes badly hurt the dogs. ; cream money: Money from selling cream was the grocery money and paid for extras like going dancing. ; harvest table: A long four-foot-wide board table at the Egberts' just for the harvest men to eat on. ; above ground cellar: Held lined-up jars of fruit, bins of potatoes and apples, and vegetables, torn down long ago. ; blacksmith work: Her father was skilled at blacksmith work, welding and fashioning steel parts they could not buy. ; custom plowing: Her husband earned extra money plowing with the first tractor in the neighborhood, working winters when other farmers waited for spring. ; gentleman farmers: Local grain farmers work very hard in summer but travel to Hawaii all winter, unlike the daylight-to-dark farmers she reads about. ; header bed: What Dan had to drive, along with caring for horses, for the three-dollar harvest wage. ; sharp-shod: Every icy morning the blacksmith sharpened protrusions on the horseshoes so they would bite into the ice on the north-slope hill. ; stock carrots: Carrots grown for the cows that she and her sister had to weed and thin. ; Washburn and Wilson: The pea-canning operation where Ella picked peas on night shifts until it closed or sold out. ; buck rake: She operated a buck rake while helping her father with haying on the farm. ; butter check: Her father's cows' cream or butter check carried the family through the Depression when neighbors lost farms over taxes. ; hay fork: She worked in the field, loading the wagon with the hay fork. ; heifer calf: Each child received a heifer calf at age ten, building a small herd whose steer calves were sold to fund college. ; John Deere: Her son Harry Eugene works with farm machinery with John Deere. ; mothering the cows: Mothering the cows was letting calves get with the right cows while the herd rested and grazed during the drive. ; Pure Line: The pea plant that came in after Washburn and Wilson, where Ella worked until she quit in 1954. ; rabbit drives: They used to have rabbit drives, the day after meeting her husband she shot rabbits with a pistol at 25 feet. ; sod schoolhouse: Her first day of school was in a sod schoolhouse back in Kansas. ; steam-tractor machines: Her father ran the steam-tractor machines in summer along with his warehouse and farm work. ; stone ball: Helena's father pulled a horse-drawn stone ball to haul sticks and debris while clearing their farm. ; stone boat: A horse-drawn sledge fitted with barrels for hauling household water from springs or railroad ditches. ; Theta County Grain Growers: Her husband worked at the grain warehouse and became manager, staying until age 65 when his legs played out. ; timberwolf: She encountered a timberwolf on a walk through snow near pasture, it passed through the stock toward the hills. ; Tramway Warehouse: Her father operated the grain warehouse as Tramway Warehouse Operator for forty-four years and ran steam tractors summers. ; wagon box: Her grandfather put out a wagon box to trap prairie chickens in the early homestead days.

Depression = the Depression | Great Depression | the first depression: They got by with a cow, pig, chickens and garden, wheat brought 21 or 22 cents, and they sold apples on the street with little money but ate. ; fire = the fire: She knows it only from books, centered more around Wallace than Kellogg, men surveying the fire got down in the water by a bridge as it closed in. ; World War II = World War Two: She lived at Fort Lewis while her husband guarded German prisoners, she recalls blacked-out trains and fears of attack on the Washington coast. ; World War I = World War One: Harry served in medical service in France amputating limbs, she stopped school to carry the mail when her physics class emptied. ; welfare: She went on welfare to return to school, and later disapproved of the system after renting to women on it. ; flu epidemic = flu: The 1918 flu twice closed the school where she taught at eighteen, she ran the ailing photographer's studio for ten days. ; washing machine payments = washing machine: During the Depression she could not scrape $5 to pay on her washing machine and barely kept it. ; relief: The family drew free government food while her husband worked limited hours on Troy's sewer project, she says many on relief don't need it. ; Pearl Harbor = December 7, 1941: Her brother graduated around Pearl Harbor and served four years, she was working at the hardware store when war broke out. ; the flood = January flood: Tap water ran mud that she strained, boiled, and chlorinated, one flood put five and a half feet of water in her home and forced moving the house. ; Korean War: Her son served on a destroyer bombing oil stockpiles off Korea in 1952, her brother left college for four Navy years. ; 1910 fire = great Idaho fire: Her mother buried the dishes and fled with the children, she carried her baby and a sheet of diapers while men were pulled off streets to fight it. ; Civilian Conservation Corps = C C C's | CCC camps | CCs: City boys from New York, Chicago and Philadelphia sent west for forest work, they shouldered open a snowed-in road and built roads near Avery. ; Expo '74 = Expo: The family had season tickets and attended nearly every weekend to escape the lead, enjoying its cultural offerings. ; food stamps: She criticizes how people obtain food stamps and believes the program is abused. ; Seattle World's Fair = Seattle Fair: They went by train and she liked it less than Spokane's, she cooked for the British consul in Seattle that summer. ; GI Bill: She regrets not entering the service, since with the GI Bill she could have furthered the education she paid for herself. ; WPA: The local relief program predated national relief, men were put on WPA work to earn enough for food. ; Spokane Fair: She much preferred it to Seattle's, with more to see and do, her daughter's family spent a whole wonderful day there. ; buying on credit: Her parents never charged anything or bought on credit, a value carried from the Depression. ; big fires: During big fires all the men were out firefighting and the women stayed alone with the children. ; G.I. Bill: Asked whether her brothers used it, she describes one weighing college after the service. ; blizzard of 88: She went through the blizzard of 1888 in South Dakota, and another later in North Dakota. ; gas rationing: She met her husband during wartime gas rationing, when he delivered eggs to the hatchery. ; Vietnam: Both husbands served two years and returned to indifference—there was no glory, unlike World War II. ; air watch: During World War Two local women staffed the air watch, calling in aircraft sightings to a central number. ; land use planning: She opposes land use planning as government control over owners' property, unless legislated locally. ; Skywatch: Wartime plane-spotting program in which she volunteered 500 hours, earning Air Force life membership, wings and a medal. ; cyclone: A cyclone blew off the farmhouse roof, felled the windmill, and drove a twenty-pound weight where her mother had sat. ; New Deal: She credits Roosevelt's New Deal government jobs, then argues the dole broke the back of American independence. ; rainmakers: When she was a child, rainmakers were hired to shoot the clouds to make it rain, but they had no result. ; air raid drills: During World War Two her Lewiston schoolchildren crawled under desks for air raid drills. ; Compton I. White: The congressman who came to her door to congratulate her as the best census taker in Idaho. ; Eisenhower's inauguration: She traveled to Washington, D.C. and watched the parade from a bench for hours. ; Federal Disaster Protection Act of 1973: Floods brought flood plain zoning under this act, administered by HUD, restricting building on the flood plain. ; foster care = foster parents: Because Boise had no foster parents for handicapped children, publicity brought ten families to apply to take the narrator's son. ; ration stamps: Wartime stamps limited how much sugar, gas, and other goods people could get, making living rough. ; secondhand TV: Bought for $285 with only $25 trade-in, ending up costing over $300 through a finance company. ; WACs: She joined in the war years to return to school on the GI Bill and out of adventurous spirit. ; 4th of July picnics: As a child the family always went, and her father raced his little horse against the other boys. ; bank day at high school: Every Tuesday students banked their nickels and pennies, her savings were lost when the banks closed. ; blackout: During the war trains ran with coach shades drawn down for blackout. ; bond drive: She received a commendation for her bond drive work during the Second World War. ; Department of Civil Defense, Department of the Army: It gave her an award for the Pomeroy work. ; Department of Health and Welfare: Her office space during the flood response was in the back of its building. ; eruption of Mount St. Helens: She counts the March and May 18th eruptions among the remarkable events of her lifetime. ; flag the train: The little local passenger train would stop practically anywhere, riders flagged it down and asked to be let off at their place. ; GI loan: Her foster son used his GI loan together with her Potlatch wages to finish university after the war. ; Gold Rush in '49: Her father and one of her mother's brothers went to the California Gold Rush of 1849. ; hand-me-down dresses: During the Depression schoolchildren wore hand-me-down dresses, and graduates made their own. ; Inland Empire Division: She is a volunteer disaster consultant for it, covering parts of Idaho and Washington. ; Santa Fe Railroad: Her father worked building spurs for it before she was born on the prairie. ; soup kitchens: She recalls transients came through during the Depression and there was desperate need of soup kitchens. ; troop train: Crowded wartime train her family boarded in Omaha, forcing her mother to ride the steps between cars overnight. ; war bonds: The war bond program took money from her brother's pay each month to save for him. ; Washington Civil Defense: The head of the state civil defense signed her award for the Pomeroy flood work.

canning = canning meat: Narrators can everything with pressure cookers, valuing full shelves as visible accomplishment, unlike housework. ; hunting: Hunting was done mainly from responsibility, to have meat canned and stored against layoffs, not just for sport. ; midwife = midwifery | midwifery practice: Midwives came for days when babies were born at home, narrators' mothers rode out with doctors to deliver babies, refusing to put a money value on the work. ; natural childbirth: She had all three children naturally, without spinal pain killers, and says she would choose that way again. ; sex education: One narrator had her daughter taken out of school sex education classes, another learned about sex from watching animals on the farm. ; huckleberry picking: Women picked huckleberries around camps and sold a pail for a dollar or to tourists. ; birth control pills: A priest finally agreed the Catholic narrator could use them after her fourth child, another narrator fears the pill causes cancer. ; hops: Dried hops boiled into a strong tea and drunk for two or three days was said to drive off the flu. ; cottage cheese: Made by souring milk in a big granite pan, heating without boiling, and straining off the whey, she sold it. ; Carla Emery: A young Kendrick woman self-publishing a book on country living, gossiped about for neglecting her five children. ; peppermint: Used as a cooling ointment or tea for burns and as a medicine children would take joyfully with sugar. ; catnip: Given generally to a child who did not feel good, like peppermint. ; old time remedies: She wrote a list of about 25 old-time farmer remedies used when people couldn't get to a doctor. ; onion poultice: Onions fried in grease, wrapped in a dish towel and laid hot on the chest, she calls mighty against pneumonia. ; dehydrator: An electric four-shelf appliance she uses to dry garden produce and make jerky, preferring freezing to canning. ; tatting: She did quite a bit of tatting along with embroidery, crocheting and knitting, learned partly from a Swede woman. ; quinine: Given for ague, the doctor bribed the child with a two-cent piece to take it. ; witch hazel: Rubbed on aching hips to soothe them. ; ague: An old ailment of terrible headache with alternating fever and chills, treated with quinine. ; can milk: Canned milk was all they had for cooking before they got their first cow. ; mustard plaster: The mustard plaster was valued because it drew the sickness right out. ; polio epidemic: Children were crippled and dying during the epidemic, and her son was isolated with suspected polio. ; rhubarb: Used as a remedy, either the top or the center part usually stewed in spring. ; sassafras tea: Drunk in springtime, some liked it so much they used it instead of China tea at the table. ; scarlet fever: Her son was kept in bed six weeks while two doctors visited every evening without charging. ; wild cherry bark: When a doctor was fifty or a hundred miles off, a sick man drank cherry bark tea in bed a few days and returned to work. ; soaking game in vinegar = soak it in vinegar | tomato juice: To take the wild taste out of game meat you soak it in vinegar, and tomato juice or anything acid takes skunk smell out of clothes. ; carbuncle: A boil with smaller boils around it, one of the old-time ailments she defines. ; croup: An aggravated form of tonsillitis, a word the speaker has not heard for years. ; Smith Brothers cough drops: Remembered as a great remedy in old times. ; two cent piece: Coin the doctor offered her if she would take her medicine, larger and thicker than a penny. ; smokehouse: They built a little building and hung meat in it to smoke. ; Cesarean abortion: As a Hailey nurse she gave anesthetics while a doctor performed abortions, including a Cesarean on a girl farther along. ; cocoa butter: Describes cocoa butter balls used in the 1930s as a blocking contraceptive that melts at body temperature. ; cooking for the hunters: She cooks for as many as 22 or 23 hunters, favoring spaghetti or stew that can be warmed over for late groups. ; Rose Hours Bakery: Hollis worked there one summer selling food, clerking, and cleaning up. ; blood sausage: They butchered weekly, used the whole hog, and made blood sausage and pickled pigs' feet for the sausage route. ; cougar meat: The boys eat cougar and bear steaks, she says cougar tastes like pork, though Bob will not touch it. ; diphtheria = diptheria: Her older sister died of diphtheria and Leah caught it from her, surviving, the family said, through prayer. ; dried beef: Without cold storage the family cured butchered meat into dried, chipped beef for school sandwiches. ; hepatitis epidemic: Bad water at the camp brought hepatitis to 19 of 36 people. ; miners' consumption: Her father's miners' consumption was actually emphysema from heavy copper settling in his lungs in the Butte mines. ; yogurt: She makes her own yogurt at home rather than buying prepared foods. ; born at home with a midwife: The narrator was born at home in 1914 with a midwife attending, though her own children were born in hospitals. ; butter churning: They milked many cows and she was always churning butter on the farm. ; dried prunes: She dries prunes in the oven and freezer-packs them in zip-lock bags to serve later. ; Rocky Mountain oysters: Deep-fat-fried breaded sheep's testicles, tasting like a cross between a scallop and liver. ; salt rising bread: Carla Emery's country living book tells how to make salt rising bread and home brewed beverages. ; Bean Loaf: Boiled beans ground with cheap cuts like pig's feet, spiced, baked, and served with gravy broth. ; beef jerky: They make their own, which her husband dries. ; bottle feeding: Doctors of her mother's generation really encouraged bottle feeding and mothers were put out to give birth in the hospital. ; botulism: They never heard about botulism. ; cheeses: She makes her own cheeses at home from their raw milk. ; copper kettle: They filled an old copper boiler half full of jelly their first year and ended up with jelly spilled on the floor. ; Dale Davis' book: A Dale Davis book on natural foods got her started, then she learned butter and yogurt making from other books. ; dill pickles: She still cans dill pickles, now nearly the only thing the household puts up. ; granola: She makes her own granola at home. ; grub box: Men took the grub box with tools, gear and horses up to cut all their winter wood. ; oatmeal bread: When war made white flour and sugar scarce she used honey and made oatmeal bread just as good. ; pressure cookers: They didn't have pressure cookers until later, they had to boil it for hours. ; sarmas: Meat, rice, and other things rolled in little cabbage leaves, made for family gatherings. ; slates: Students in the one-room school wrote on slates and washed them with bottles of water. ; sourdough cooking: One of her creative-cooking pursuits, alongside winemaking.

electricity: The big improvement on the farm, coming some twenty years after marriage, before that she pumped and carried water. ; wood stove: The homestead cabin's heat and cooking came from a wood stove, she learned to heat water and build fires while her husband worked. ; ice cream: She makes her own ice cream from their raw milk. ; covered wagon: Her family crossed the plains in a covered wagon with oxen, she traveled from Curlew to Camas County by covered wagon in 1919. ; walking the railroad tracks = railroad tracks: As children they walked the railroad tracks to and from Miltown rather than the road, something no one would do now. ; paper dolls = catalog: They cut paper dolls by the hundreds out of the catalogs, and her sister made beautiful paper doll clothes. ; outdoor toilet = outhouse: They had no indoor plumbing until 1946 and used the outdoor toilet even at 25 below zero. ; trailer house: In fifth grade they lived in a little trailer house with an outhouse, hauling hot water in a bucket to wash dishes. ; fancy work = drawn handwork | needlepoint with cotton: Grandmothers taught needlework, drawn handwork and crocheting, narrators still keep up fancy work as a hobby. ; icebox = ice boxes: They finally got ice boxes and put ice in them, the family had one before their first refrigerator. ; kerosene lamps: She had eight lamps to clean every two or three days before electricity, she was scared to death of gas light. ; phonograph: Her first phonograph, with a big horn, played for a nickel in her mother's hotel dining room. ; pinochle: Teachers in the company house played pinochle through winter evenings, she plays with children, grandchildren and neighbors. ; river steamboats = Flyer | Georgie Oaks: The Flyer, Georgie Oaks and Idaho ran daily from Coeur d'Alene upriver to St. Mary's carrying many passengers. ; sawdust: Ice was stacked and covered with sawdust to keep it almost all summer. ; ringer washer: Her mother had a ringer washer, one of few appliances in her childhood home. ; stages: Before they had a car they rode to town on stages, big touring cars run by local people. ; washboard: She washed clothes on a washboard keeping house for her father, her daughter later found one and did not know what it was. ; corset: Lined, with steel or whalebone strips in pockets, laced tightly up the back with a strong tape. ; respirator: Local women bought one and took a Red Cross course, miners must now carry an oxygen deal good for about an hour. ; treadle machine = treadle sewing machines: She sewed all her children's clothes on a treadle machine until they were about ten, then bought an electric. ; artesian well: The town put down an artesian well, then a new and unusual thing, and the family hauled water from it by wagon. ; turntable: She describes her father turning the railroad turntable by hand to move an engine to the right track. ; wood cook stove: She carried and chopped wood for it as a girl and a wife, and still misses firing it up to bake bread. ; wooden sidewalks: When she first came, Potlatch had all wooden sidewalks and company houses kept up by a painting crew. ; Delco plant = Delco system: A diesel generator giving a teacher's cabin or ranger station lights in the early evening, with no telephone or radio. ; dynamite boxes: They used dynamite boxes for furniture while waiting three months for ordered pieces, her father built her a playhouse from them. ; flat iron: Old flat irons had to be gripped with a thick cloth until Mrs. Potts's removable-handle model came in about 1875. ; windmill: What they had to get to pump the well water after striking a stream they could not lower. ; Sears and Roebuck catalog = wish book: The wish book: girls cut pretty girls from the big catalog to make their own paper dolls. ; straw ticks: They made mattresses out of ticking filled with straw. ; tar soap: They used big black tar soap for shampoo. ; flour sacks: They made underwear, dresses, aprons, and even bras out of flour sacks. ; warming oven: Wood-stove warming ovens kept bread and rolls warm while the rest of the meal cooked. ; wringer washer: In the cabin she heated water in a tank on the wood stove and drained it into an old wringer washer. ; curling irons: Heated in a lamp to curl bobbed hair. ; generators: During the flood outage a brother-in-law came around with a generator to plug in freezers so people did not lose food. ; hobble skirt: She had to pull herself up onto the tall step of the greasy logging engine while wearing a hobble skirt. ; orange crates for furniture: The interviewer recalls and she confirms that newlyweds first starting out had orange crates for furniture. ; ringer washing machine: As a child she helped with the washing, dragging the old ringer washing machine in and out. ; service berries: Service berries grow on the hills all around the area and look similar to blueberries. ; sifter: A covered, pumped container they filled with water packed in a barrel from Black Rock before the well. ; standing collars: At the end of the 1800s women made and wore standing collars, and men's shirts had collars buttoned on separately. ; taffy pulling: Children pulled taffy at parties, each given a piece to roll in flour and pull until it turned white. ; wool cards: Flat paddles studded with nails used to pull wool fibers apart and clean out seeds before washing. ; airtight stove: The stove she tended while alone with a new baby in a house that was just a shell when bought. ; Atwater Kent: The first radio in Avery, others gathered nightly to hear it despite an awful lot of static. ; battery radio: With no electricity the battery had to be rationed, and it died the day of Pearl Harbor. ; big walk-in icebox: The pantry women kept trays of turkey sandwiches, milkshakes, and fruit salad in it for late feeds. ; caboose stove: Marble Creek Station kept an old round caboose stove and fuel so waiting passengers could keep warm in winter. ; circulating wood stove: They bought one that could hold wood and keep fire most of the night. ; corset cover: Often trimmed with homemade embroidery or lace, extending from the top of the corset to the hips. ; daisy chain: Her grandmother taught her to weave daisies and dandelions together in the spring. ; feather beds: At her grandmother's she slept in great big feather beds, two deep, so soft a hand left an imprint. ; flannel bloomers: Her mother made nearly all their clothes, she hated the flannel bloomers but they were warm for the long walk to school. ; fox and geese: Children trampled fox and geese and dog and deer trail games into the snow in winter. ; hand washing machine: Recalling childhood chores, she mentions doing dishes and clothes with a hand washing machine. ; mud butter: Indians smeared mud butter over prairie chickens, cooked them on a bonfire, and pulled feathers off to eat them. ; natural dyeing: Dyeing wool with plants, the daughter's three-year science fair project that won the Grand Award in Spokane. ; party lines: Farmers owned their own telephone companies with a central and party lines carrying fifteen to forty people. ; player piano: She has had a little organ, a piano, and a player piano and entertains herself with them. ;
